name: Formation of the Earth
summary: Earth accreted from the solar nebula roughly 4.5 billion years ago, a molten world bombarded by planetesimals.
body:
Dust and rock orbiting the young Sun accreted into planetesimals and then into the proto-Earth over a few tens of millions of years. The heat of accretion and radioactive decay kept the surface molten, and iron sank to form the core while lighter silicates floated up as the mantle and first crust.

Radiometric dating of meteorites and the oldest terrestrial zircons fixes the age at roughly **4.54 billion years** — the floor of this timeline.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_Earth).

name: Giant impact forms the Moon
summary: A Mars-sized body, Theia, struck the proto-Earth; debris from the collision coalesced into the Moon.
body:
The collision melted much of the planet, stripped away a large fraction of the mantle and left Earth with an unusually large satellite and a strong axial tilt.

The Moon stabilises Earth's obliquity, which has kept the climate comparatively steady over billions of years — a precondition for the [origin of life](event:abiogenesis).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Giant-impact_hypothesis).

name: First oceans
summary: Water condensed onto a cooling crust, forming the first liquid oceans.
body:
Zircon crystals from the Jack Hills of Western Australia carry an oxygen-isotope signature suggesting liquid water existed within about 150 million years of Earth's formation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_of_water_on_Earth).

name: Late Heavy Bombardment
summary: A surge of asteroid impacts scarred the inner Solar System, cratering the Moon and resurfacing the young Earth.
body:
The Moon's great impact basins cluster in this interval, which is why it is inferred for Earth as well; the terrestrial craters have long since been erased by erosion and plate tectonics.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Heavy_Bombardment).

name: Origin of life
summary: Self-replicating chemistry appeared, most likely around hydrothermal systems, giving rise to the first cells.
body:
The earliest widely accepted chemical traces of life are carbon-isotope signatures in rocks around **3.8 billion years** old, with unambiguous microfossils and [stromatolites](event:stromatolites) not long after.

Every organism alive today descends from a single population, the last universal common ancestor.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abiogenesis).

name: Earliest stromatolites
summary: Layered microbial mats in Western Australia preserve some of the oldest direct evidence of life.
body:
Part of [Origin of life](event:abiogenesis). The Dresser and Strelley Pool formations of the Pilbara craton preserve laminated structures built by microbial communities in shallow water.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stromatolite).

name: Oxygenic photosynthesis evolves
summary: Cyanobacteria learned to split water with sunlight, releasing free oxygen as waste.
body:
This single metabolic innovation eventually rebuilt the atmosphere, the oceans and the chemistry of the crust, leading directly to the [Great Oxidation Event](event:great-oxidation).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Photosynthesis).

name: Great Oxidation Event
summary: Free oxygen accumulated in the atmosphere for the first time, poisoning most existing life and rusting the planet.
body:
Oxygen produced by [cyanobacteria](event:oxygenic-photosynthesis) had for hundreds of millions of years been absorbed by dissolved iron, laying down banded iron formations. Once those sinks were saturated, oxygen escaped into the air.

The consequences were enormous: an ozone layer formed, methane greenhouse warming collapsed into the [Huronian glaciation](event:huronian-glaciation), and aerobic respiration — far more energetic than fermentation — became possible.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Oxidation_Event).

name: Huronian glaciation
summary: The first known global glaciation, triggered when rising oxygen destroyed atmospheric methane.
body:
Part of [Great Oxidation Event](event:great-oxidation). Glacial deposits near Lake Huron in Ontario give the event its name. It may have been the longest ice age in Earth history, lasting some 300 million years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Huronian_glaciation).

name: First eukaryotic cells
summary: One cell engulfed another and kept it; the result was the complex, compartmented cell with mitochondria.
body:
Endosymbiosis gave eukaryotes an internal power plant and, with it, the energy budget to support large genomes, large cells and eventually multicellular bodies. Chloroplasts arrived by the same route somewhat later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eukaryote).

name: Rodinia supercontinent
summary: Nearly all continental crust gathered into a single landmass before rifting apart again.
body:
Its break-up flooded the world with shallow seas and increased silicate weathering, which may have helped tip the planet into [Snowball Earth](event:snowball-earth).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rodinia).

name: Snowball Earth
summary: Glaciers reached the tropics — possibly the whole ocean froze over — in the Cryogenian period.
body:
The Sturtian and Marinoan glaciations buried much of the planet in ice for tens of millions of years. Volcanic CO2 slowly built up beneath the ice until a runaway greenhouse thawed the world in a geological instant.

The extreme environmental swings immediately preceded the appearance of the [Ediacaran biota](event:ediacaran) and the [Cambrian explosion](event:cambrian-explosion).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Snowball_Earth).

name: Ediacaran biota
summary: The first large, soft-bodied multicellular organisms appear in the fossil record.
body:
Named after the Ediacara Hills of South Australia, these fronds, discs and quilted forms are hard to place on the tree of life; most vanished at the start of the Cambrian.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ediacaran_biota).

name: Cambrian explosion
summary: Almost every modern animal body plan appears in the fossil record within a few tens of millions of years.
body:
Eyes, hard shells, jointed limbs and active predation all show up together; the Burgess Shale of British Columbia and the Chengjiang biota of Yunnan preserve the results in exquisite detail.

The trigger is debated — rising oxygen after [Snowball Earth](event:snowball-earth), the invention of predation, or genetic innovations in developmental regulation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cambrian_explosion).

name: Ordovician–Silurian extinction
summary: Roughly 85% of marine species died as glaciation locked up seawater and drained the shallow shelves.
body:
The second-largest mass extinction by species loss, it struck a world whose life was almost entirely marine.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Ordovician_mass_extinction).

name: Plants colonise the land
summary: Spore-bearing plants moved out of the water, beginning the greening of the continents.
body:
Rooting systems accelerated chemical weathering and drew down atmospheric CO2; soils, and with them terrestrial ecosystems, became possible for the first time.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evolutionary_history_of_plants).

name: Vertebrates walk on land
summary: Lobe-finned fish with weight-bearing limbs, such as Tiktaalik, ventured onto the shore.
body:
Every amphibian, reptile, bird and mammal — including us — descends from this transition, recorded in Devonian rocks of the Canadian Arctic and Greenland.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tetrapod).

name: Late Devonian extinction
summary: A drawn-out series of pulses wiped out most reef ecosystems and much of the shallow marine fauna.
body:
Expanding land plants may have driven nutrient runoff and ocean anoxia.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Devonian_extinction).

name: Carboniferous coal forests
summary: Vast swamp forests of lycopod trees buried enormous quantities of carbon that became the world's coal.
body:
Atmospheric oxygen peaked near 35%, allowing dragonflies with 70 cm wingspans. The coal laid down here fuelled the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution) 300 million years later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carboniferous_rainforest_collapse).

name: Pangaea supercontinent
summary: Nearly all land assembled into a single supercontinent surrounded by the Panthalassic Ocean.
body:
Its interior was a vast arid desert, and its coastline was short relative to its area, which stressed shallow-marine life. The break-up beginning in the Jurassic opened the [Atlantic Ocean](event:atlantic-opening) and set the continents on the paths they still follow.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pangaea).

name: Permian–Triassic extinction
summary: The Great Dying: about 81% of marine species and 70% of land vertebrates disappeared, the worst crisis life has faced.
body:
Volcanism of the [Siberian Traps](event:siberian-traps) injected enormous volumes of CO2 and sulphur into the atmosphere, driving warming, ocean acidification and widespread anoxia.

Recovery took some **10 million years**, and the emptied world was the one in which the [first dinosaurs](event:first-dinosaurs) arose.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Permian–Triassic_extinction_event).

name: Siberian Traps eruptions
summary: One of the largest volcanic events known covered millions of square kilometres of Siberia in basalt.
body:
Part of [Permian–Triassic extinction](event:permian-extinction). The lavas burned through coal and evaporite deposits, releasing carbon and halogens far beyond what the magma alone would have supplied.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siberian_Traps).

name: First dinosaurs
summary: Small bipedal archosaurs in what is now Argentina mark the beginning of the dinosaur lineage.
body:
They remained minor players until the [end-Triassic extinction](event:triassic-extinction) cleared their competitors, after which they dominated terrestrial ecosystems for 135 million years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dinosaur).

name: Triassic–Jurassic extinction
summary: Half of known species vanished as the Central Atlantic Magmatic Province erupted during the break-up of Pangaea.
body:
The survivors included the dinosaurs, which radiated into the vacated niches.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triassic–Jurassic_extinction_event).

name: Opening of the Atlantic
summary: Rifting split Pangaea and a new ocean basin began to spread along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge.
body:
Part of [Pangaea supercontinent](event:pangaea). Seafloor spreading of a few centimetres a year still widens the Atlantic today; the symmetric magnetic stripes on either side of the ridge were key evidence for plate tectonics.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_Ocean).

name: Archaeopteryx and the first birds
summary: Feathered theropods in the Jurassic lagoons of Solnhofen show dinosaurs on the way to becoming birds.
body:
Birds are living dinosaurs — the only branch of the lineage to survive the [end-Cretaceous extinction](event:kpg-extinction).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Archaeopteryx).

name: Rise of flowering plants
summary: Angiosperms appeared and, in partnership with insect pollinators, rapidly came to dominate the world's flora.
body:
Darwin called their sudden abundance in the fossil record an "abominable mystery".

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flowering_plant).

name: Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction
summary: Three quarters of all species, including every non-avian dinosaur, died out in a geological instant.
body:
The immediate cause was the [Chicxulub impact](event:chicxulub), whose ejecta blanketed the globe in an iridium-rich layer found at the boundary worldwide; the [Deccan Traps](event:deccan-traps) eruptions were already stressing ecosystems.

The extinction opened the ecological space in which mammals — and eventually [primates](event:hominin-split) — radiated.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cretaceous–Paleogene_extinction_event).

name: Chicxulub impact
summary: A 10-kilometre asteroid struck the Yucatán platform, releasing energy equal to billions of Hiroshima bombs.
body:
Part of [Cretaceous–Paleogene extinction](event:kpg-extinction). The impact excavated a crater 180 km across into sulphur-rich carbonate rock, launching a global cloud of dust and sulphate aerosols that shut down photosynthesis for years.

The crater was identified from gravity anomalies in the 1970s and confirmed in 1991.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicxulub_crater).

name: Deccan Traps eruptions
summary: Flood basalts poured over western India around the same time as the Chicxulub impact.
body:
Flood basalts poured over western India for hundreds of thousands of years either side of the [K–Pg boundary](event:kpg-extinction). Whether they were a co-cause of the extinction or merely a stressor remains actively debated.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deccan_Traps).

name: Paleocene–Eocene Thermal Maximum
summary: A massive carbon release warmed the planet by 5–8 °C within a few thousand years.
body:
The closest geological analogue to modern [greenhouse warming](event:global-warming), it acidified the oceans and drove a rapid turnover of mammal faunas.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paleocene–Eocene_Thermal_Maximum).

name: Uplift of the Himalaya
summary: India collided with Asia, raising the highest mountains on Earth and reshaping global climate.
body:
The collision continues today at about 5 cm per year. Weathering of the fresh rock drew down atmospheric CO2, helping cool the planet toward the ice ages, and the range created the Asian monsoon.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Himalayas).

name: Antarctica freezes
summary: Falling CO2 and the opening of the Drake Passage let permanent ice sheets form at the South Pole.
body:
The Eocene–Oligocene transition marks the switch from a greenhouse to an icehouse Earth, the state we still live in.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antarctic_ice_sheet).

name: Messinian salinity crisis
summary: The Mediterranean was cut off from the Atlantic and largely evaporated, leaving kilometre-thick salt deposits.
body:
It refilled catastrophically through the Strait of Gibraltar in the Zanclean flood, possibly within a couple of years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Messinian_salinity_crisis).

name: Human–chimpanzee divergence
summary: The lineages leading to humans and to chimpanzees parted ways in Africa.
body:
Fossils such as Sahelanthropus from Chad sit near this branching point; the split date comes from combining fossils with molecular clocks.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chimpanzee–human_last_common_ancestor).

name: Australopithecus and habitual bipedalism
summary: The skeleton known as Lucy showed that upright walking preceded the large human brain by millions of years.
body:
Part of [Human–chimpanzee divergence](event:hominin-split). Discovered at Hadar in Ethiopia in 1974, Lucy belongs to *Australopithecus afarensis*; the Laetoli footprints in Tanzania record the same gait in volcanic ash.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucy_(Australopithecus)).

name: First stone tools
summary: Hominins began deliberately flaking stone into cutting edges, the start of the archaeological record.
body:
The Lomekwi 3 site in Kenya pushes toolmaking back to 3.3 million years; the Oldowan industry from about 2.6 Ma is the first widespread tradition.

Stone tools gave access to meat and marrow, an energy-dense diet linked to later brain expansion.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oldowan).

name: Quaternary ice ages begin
summary: Northern hemisphere ice sheets began advancing and retreating on orbital cycles.
body:
Roughly fifty glacial–interglacial cycles, paced by Milankovitch variations in Earth's orbit, shaped the landscapes and the human evolution of the last 2.6 million years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternary_glaciation).

name: Homo erectus spreads out of Africa
summary: The first hominin with modern body proportions ranged from Africa to Java and northern China.
body:
Its long success — well over a million years — makes it the most durable human species yet known.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_erectus).

name: Control of fire
summary: Hominins learned to make and maintain fire, transforming diet, safety and social life.
body:
Burnt bone and ash at Wonderwerk Cave in South Africa give some of the earliest good evidence. Cooking releases far more calories from food and may have underwritten the expansion of the human brain.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Control_of_fire_by_early_humans).

name: Origin of Homo sapiens
summary: Anatomically modern humans emerged in Africa; the oldest known fossils come from Jebel Irhoud in Morocco.
body:
Genetic and fossil evidence points to a pan-African origin rather than a single cradle, with populations exchanging genes across the continent for tens of thousands of years before the [dispersal out of Africa](event:out-of-africa).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homo_sapiens).

name: Toba supereruption
summary: The largest volcanic eruption of the last two million years covered South Asia in ash.
body:
The proposed "Toba catastrophe" bottleneck in human populations is now largely doubted, but the volcanic winter was real and severe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toba_catastrophe_theory).

name: Out of Africa dispersal
summary: Modern humans expanded out of Africa and, within tens of millennia, reached every habitable continent.
body:
The descendants of this comparatively small founding population replaced or absorbed all other human groups, interbreeding with [Neanderthals](event:neanderthals) and Denisovans along the way.

By 65,000 years ago people had crossed to [Australia](event:sahul); by 16,000 they had entered [the Americas](event:americas-peopling).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_human_migrations).

name: Peopling of Australia
summary: Humans crossed open water to Sahul, the joined landmass of Australia and New Guinea.
body:
Part of [Out of Africa dispersal](event:out-of-africa). Madjedbebe rock shelter in Arnhem Land holds the oldest securely dated artefacts. The crossing required deliberate seafaring across at least 90 km of open ocean.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prehistory_of_Australia).

name: Neanderthals disappear
summary: The last Neanderthal populations, in Iberia and the Caucasus, died out after millennia of coexistence with modern humans.
body:
Part of [Out of Africa dispersal](event:out-of-africa). They buried their dead, used fire and pigment, and left 1–2% of their DNA in all non-African people alive today.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal).

name: Upper Paleolithic cave art
summary: Painted caves at Chauvet, Lascaux and Sulawesi show symbolic thought in full flower.
body:
The Chauvet lions and rhinos are around 36,000 years old; hand stencils and animal figures of similar age occur in Indonesia, showing the practice was not a European invention.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cave_painting).

name: Last Glacial Maximum
summary: Ice sheets reached their greatest extent and sea level stood about 125 metres below today's.
body:
The exposed shelves created land bridges — Beringia, Doggerland, Sundaland — that shaped where humans could walk.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last_Glacial_Maximum).

name: Peopling of the Americas
summary: Humans crossed Beringia and moved south along the Pacific coast into two empty continents.
body:
Part of [Out of Africa dispersal](event:out-of-africa). Sites such as Monte Verde in Chile predate the Clovis culture, implying an earlier coastal route; within a few thousand years people had reached Tierra del Fuego.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Settlement_of_the_Americas).

name: Domestication of the dog
summary: Wolves became the first domesticated animal, thousands of years before any crop or livestock.
body:
The Bonn-Oberkassel burial of about 14,200 years ago includes a dog interred with two people.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Origin_of_the_domestic_dog).

name: Younger Dryas cold snap
summary: The warming world plunged back into near-glacial conditions for over a millennium, then warmed again within decades.
body:
Its end defines the start of the [Holocene](event:holocene) and coincides with the first experiments in [farming](event:agriculture) in the Levant.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Younger_Dryas).

name: Start of the Holocene
summary: The current interglacial began, ushering in the stable warm climate in which all civilisation developed.
body:
The boundary is defined in a Greenland ice core; temperatures rose several degrees within a few decades.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holocene).

name: Dawn of agriculture
summary: Farming was invented independently in several regions, beginning with the Fertile Crescent, and permanently changed how humans live.
body:
Wheat, barley, peas, sheep and goats were domesticated in the hills of the Levant and upper Mesopotamia; rice in the Yangtze valley, maize in Mexico, potatoes in the Andes.

Food surpluses allowed permanent villages, storable wealth, specialists and eventually cities — but also poorer diets, epidemic disease and hierarchy. Everything from [writing](event:writing) to the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution) rests on this foundation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic_Revolution).

name: Göbekli Tepe
summary: Hunter-gatherers raised monumental carved pillars in southeastern Anatolia, before pottery or farming villages.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). Circles of T-shaped limestone pillars up to 5.5 m tall are decorated with foxes, snakes and vultures. The site suggests that large-scale ritual gathering may have preceded, rather than followed, settled agriculture.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Göbekli_Tepe).

name: Domestication of livestock
summary: Sheep, goats, pigs and cattle were brought under human management, followed later by the horse.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). Domestic animals supplied meat, milk, wool, traction and manure — and, in close quarters, the zoonotic diseases that would later devastate populations without immunity.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Domestication_of_animals).

name: Walls of Jericho
summary: One of the world's oldest continuously occupied settlements built a stone wall and tower.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). One of the world's oldest continuously occupied settlements built a stone wall and tower.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jericho).

name: Çatalhöyük
summary: A dense Neolithic town in Anatolia housing several thousand people in mudbrick houses entered through the roof.
body:
Part of [Dawn of agriculture](event:agriculture). A dense Neolithic town in Anatolia housing several thousand people in mudbrick houses entered through the roof.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Çatalhöyük).

name: Invention of the wheel
summary: Potters' wheels and then wheeled vehicles appeared across Mesopotamia and the Pontic steppe.
body:
The oldest wheeled-vehicle images and surviving wheels date to the fourth millennium BCE; the axle, not the wheel itself, was the hard part.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wheel).

name: Bronze Age begins
summary: Alloying copper with tin produced a metal hard enough for tools and weapons, and trade networks to carry the ingredients.
body:
Tin is rare and rarely found near copper, so bronze required long-distance exchange stretching from Cornwall and Afghanistan to the Mediterranean — a fragility that helped bring on the [Late Bronze Age collapse](event:bronze-age-collapse).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age).

name: Rise of Uruk and the first cities
summary: Uruk in southern Mesopotamia grew into arguably the world's first city, with tens of thousands of inhabitants.
body:
Monumental temples, mass-produced pottery and administrative seals mark the emergence of a state-scale society, and the accounting needs of its temples produced [writing](event:writing).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uruk).

name: Invention of writing
summary: Cuneiform accounting marks in Sumer became the first true writing system, with Egyptian hieroglyphs following within a century or two.
body:
What began as tokens for counting grain and livestock became, within a few centuries, a full script able to record law, literature and history — and with it the first records that historians can read directly.

Writing was invented independently at least three more times: in China, in Mesoamerica, and probably in the Indus valley.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_writing).

name: Unification of Egypt
summary: Upper and Lower Egypt were unified under a single king, traditionally Narmer, beginning three millennia of pharaonic civilisation.
body:
The Narmer Palette shows the king wearing the crowns of both lands. The state that emerged, bound together by the Nile, outlasted every one of its Bronze Age contemporaries.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Dynastic_Period_(Egypt)).

name: Great Pyramid of Giza
summary: Khufu's tomb, 146 metres tall and built from over two million blocks, was the tallest structure on Earth for 3,800 years.
body:
Part of [Unification of Egypt](event:egypt-unification). It is the only one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World still standing, and was raised by a paid, organised workforce rather than by slaves.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Pyramid_of_Giza).

name: Indus Valley civilisation
summary: Mohenjo-daro and Harappa held grid-planned cities with drains, standardised bricks and a script still undeciphered.
body:
At its height the civilisation covered a larger area than Egypt and Mesopotamia combined, apparently without palaces, royal tombs or obvious armies.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indus_Valley_Civilisation).

name: Stonehenge
summary: The sarsen circle was raised on Salisbury Plain, aligned on the solstice sunrise and sunset.
body:
The bluestones were dragged or carried some 250 km from the Preseli hills of Wales.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stonehenge).

name: Akkadian Empire
summary: Sargon of Akkad conquered the Sumerian cities and assembled what is often called the first empire.
body:
It ran on standing armies, appointed governors and a common language of administration — a template later empires would recognise. Drought may have brought it down.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Akkadian_Empire).

name: Code of Hammurabi
summary: The Babylonian king had 282 laws carved on a basalt stele and set up in public.
body:
It is not the earliest law code, but it is the most complete, and it fixed the principle that the law was written down and knowable rather than the king's whim of the day.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Code_of_Hammurabi).

name: Shang dynasty
summary: The first Chinese dynasty attested by contemporary writing, ruling from Anyang with bronze ritual vessels and oracle bones.
body:
Questions inscribed on ox scapulae and turtle plastrons are the ancestors of the Chinese script still in use today.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shang_dynasty).

name: Eruption of Thera
summary: One of the largest eruptions of the Holocene destroyed the Minoan town of Akrotiri on Santorini.
body:
Ash and tsunamis struck Crete, and the buried town — preserved like a Bronze Age Pompeii — has been linked, speculatively, to the legend of Atlantis.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Minoan_eruption).

name: Vedic period in India
summary: The Vedas were composed in Sanskrit, laying the foundations of Hindu religion, ritual and social order.
body:
The Vedas were composed in Sanskrit, laying the foundations of Hindu religion, ritual and social order.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vedic_period).

name: Battle of Kadesh
summary: Egyptians under Ramesses II fought the Hittites to a draw; the peace that followed is the earliest surviving international treaty.
body:
Egyptians under Ramesses II fought the Hittites to a draw; the peace that followed is the earliest surviving international treaty.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Kadesh).

name: Iron Age begins
summary: Ironworking spread from Anatolia across Eurasia and Africa, putting hard metal within reach of ordinary farmers and soldiers.
body:
Unlike bronze, iron ore is common almost everywhere, so the new metal broke the trade dependency that had constrained the [Bronze Age](event:bronze-age).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age).

name: Late Bronze Age collapse
summary: Within about fifty years the Hittite empire, Mycenaean Greece and the great trading cities of the Levant were all destroyed or abandoned.
body:
Ugarit, Hattusa and Pylos burned; Egypt survived but was permanently weakened after fighting off the "Sea Peoples". Drought, earthquake swarms, migration and the collapse of interlocking trade networks all seem to be involved.

Greece lost writing altogether for four centuries — a genuine dark age.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late_Bronze_Age_collapse).

name: Trojan War
summary: The legendary siege of Troy, dated by later Greeks to the twelfth century BCE and immortalised in the *Iliad*.
body:
Part of [Late Bronze Age collapse](event:bronze-age-collapse). The legendary siege of Troy, dated by later Greeks to the twelfth century BCE and immortalised in the *Iliad*.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trojan_War).

name: Phoenician alphabet
summary: A script of about 22 consonant signs, simple enough for merchants to learn, spread around the Mediterranean.
body:
Greek, Latin, Aramaic, Hebrew and Arabic all descend from it, as does — through Latin — the alphabet you are reading now.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phoenician_alphabet).

name: Solomon's Temple in Jerusalem
summary: The First Temple was built in Jerusalem, becoming the centre of Israelite worship until its destruction in 587 BCE.
body:
The First Temple was built in Jerusalem, becoming the centre of Israelite worship until its destruction in 587 BCE.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Solomon%27s_Temple).

name: Founding of Carthage
summary: Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded the city that would dominate the western Mediterranean until the [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars).
body:
Phoenician settlers from Tyre founded the city that would dominate the western Mediterranean until the [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carthage).

name: Neo-Assyrian Empire
summary: Assyria built the largest empire the world had yet seen, ruling from Nineveh with siege engines, mass deportation and a road system.
body:
Assyria built the largest empire the world had yet seen, ruling from Nineveh with siege engines, mass deportation and a road system.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neo-Assyrian_Empire).

name: First Olympic Games
summary: The traditional date of the first games at Olympia, which the Greeks used as the origin of their shared chronology.
body:
The traditional date of the first games at Olympia, which the Greeks used as the origin of their shared chronology.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ancient_Olympic_Games).

name: Founding of Rome
summary: Traditional date of Rome's founding, the seed of the republic and empire that would shape the Mediterranean world.
body:
Archaeology shows settlement on the Palatine from at least the tenth century BCE; the Romulus legend gave the city a founding myth to match its later power.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Founding_of_Rome).

name: Life of the Buddha
summary: Siddhartha Gautama taught in the Ganges plain, founding one of the world's great religious and philosophical traditions.
body:
His teaching — the Four Noble Truths and the Eightfold Path — spread with merchants and, later, with the patronage of [Ashoka](event:maurya-empire) across South, Central and East Asia.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gautama_Buddha).

name: Confucius
summary: Kong Qiu taught an ethic of duty, ritual propriety and learning that shaped Chinese government and society for two millennia.
body:
Confucian texts became the syllabus of the imperial examinations, making his thought the working philosophy of the Chinese state from the [Han](event:han-dynasty) onward.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Confucius).

name: Achaemenid Persian Empire
summary: Cyrus the Great and his successors ruled from the Aegean to the Indus, the largest empire the world had seen.
body:
The Persians governed through satrapies, a royal road, a standardised coinage and a policy of religious tolerance — Cyrus is remembered in the Hebrew Bible for allowing the Judean exiles to return.

It fell to [Alexander](event:alexander-conquests) in 330 BCE.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Achaemenid_Empire).

name: Athenian democracy
summary: The reforms of Cleisthenes gave political power to the assembly of citizens, inventing direct democracy.
body:
Roughly 30,000 adult male citizens could vote; women, resident foreigners and a very large enslaved population could not. Even so, the idea that ordinary people should decide public matters begins here.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athenian_democracy).

name: Greco-Persian Wars
summary: The Greek city-states repelled two Persian invasions, a victory that shaped Greek self-understanding for centuries.
body:
The wars produced [Marathon](event:marathon), [Thermopylae](event:thermopylae) and [Salamis](event:salamis), and their telling by Herodotus effectively invented history as a literary form.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greco-Persian_Wars).

name: Battle of Marathon
summary: An outnumbered Athenian hoplite army defeated the Persian landing force on the plain of Marathon.
body:
Part of [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars). An outnumbered Athenian hoplite army defeated the Persian landing force on the plain of Marathon.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Marathon).

name: Battle of Thermopylae
summary: Leonidas and a small Greek force held the coastal pass for three days against Xerxes' army before being outflanked.
body:
Part of [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars). Leonidas and a small Greek force held the coastal pass for three days against Xerxes' army before being outflanked.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Thermopylae).

name: Battle of Salamis
summary: The Greek fleet destroyed the larger Persian navy in the narrows off Salamis, forcing Xerxes to withdraw.
body:
Part of [Greco-Persian Wars](event:greco-persian-wars). The Greek fleet destroyed the larger Persian navy in the narrows off Salamis, forcing Xerxes to withdraw.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Salamis).

name: Parthenon built
summary: Athens crowned its Acropolis with a marble temple to Athena, paid for out of the tribute of its empire.
body:
Part of [Athenian democracy](event:athenian-democracy). Athens crowned its Acropolis with a marble temple to Athena, paid for out of the tribute of its empire.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parthenon).

name: Peloponnesian War
summary: Athens and Sparta fought for 27 years; Athens lost its fleet, its empire and, for a time, its democracy.
body:
Thucydides' account of the war is the founding text of realist political analysis.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peloponnesian_War).

name: Trial and death of Socrates
summary: Athens condemned Socrates to drink hemlock for impiety and corrupting the young.
body:
Through Plato and Aristotle his method of relentless questioning became the backbone of Western philosophy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trial_of_Socrates).

name: Aristotle
summary: Aristotle systematised logic, biology, physics, ethics and politics, and tutored the young Alexander.
body:
His works dominated European and Islamic learning until the [Scientific Revolution](event:copernicus) began to overturn them.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aristotle).

name: Conquests of Alexander the Great
summary: In eleven years Alexander destroyed the Persian Empire and led an army from Greece to the Punjab.
body:
He founded some twenty cities, [Alexandria](event:alexandria) chief among them, and after his death at 32 his generals carved the conquests into the Hellenistic kingdoms.

Greek language, art and civic forms spread from Egypt to Afghanistan and outlasted the empire that carried them there.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wars_of_Alexander_the_Great).

name: Battle of Gaugamela
summary: Alexander broke the main Persian army under Darius III, opening Mesopotamia and Persia to conquest.
body:
Part of [Conquests of Alexander the Great](event:alexander-conquests). Alexander broke the main Persian army under Darius III, opening Mesopotamia and Persia to conquest.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gaugamela).

name: Founding of Alexandria
summary: Alexander laid out a Greek city on the Egyptian coast that became the intellectual capital of the Mediterranean.
body:
Part of [Conquests of Alexander the Great](event:alexander-conquests). Its [Library and Museum](event:library-alexandria) drew scholars from across the Hellenistic world.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandria).

name: Library of Alexandria
summary: The Ptolemies assembled the greatest collection of scrolls in the ancient world and paid scholars to work on them.
body:
Part of [Founding of Alexandria](event:alexandria). Eratosthenes measured the circumference of the Earth here to within a few percent; Euclid, Archimedes and Ptolemy all worked in its orbit. The library declined over centuries rather than perishing in a single fire.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Library_of_Alexandria).

name: Mauryan Empire and Ashoka
summary: Chandragupta Maurya unified most of the Indian subcontinent; his grandson Ashoka renounced war for Buddhism.
body:
After the bloodshed of the Kalinga campaign, Ashoka had edicts of tolerance and non-violence carved on rocks and pillars across his empire, and sent [Buddhist](event:buddha) missions as far as Sri Lanka and the Hellenistic kingdoms.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maurya_Empire).

name: Qin unification of China
summary: Ying Zheng conquered the warring states and declared himself Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of a unified China.
body:
He standardised script, coinage, weights and axle widths, linked frontier walls into an early [Great Wall](event:great-wall), and was buried with the [Terracotta Army](event:terracotta-army). The dynasty lasted fifteen years; the unified state it created has recurred ever since.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qin_dynasty).

name: Great Wall of China
summary: Frontier walls were linked and repeatedly rebuilt over eighteen centuries; most of what survives is Ming work.
body:
Part of [Qin unification of China](event:qin-unification). Frontier walls were linked and repeatedly rebuilt over eighteen centuries; most of what survives is Ming work.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Wall_of_China).

name: Terracotta Army
summary: Some 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers were buried to guard the first emperor's tomb; farmers rediscovered them in 1974.
body:
Part of [Qin unification of China](event:qin-unification). Some 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers were buried to guard the first emperor's tomb; farmers rediscovered them in 1974.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terracotta_Army).

name: Punic Wars
summary: Three wars between Rome and Carthage decided who would rule the western Mediterranean.
body:
Hannibal crossed the Alps and destroyed Roman armies at [Cannae](event:cannae), but Rome outlasted him; [Scipio](event:zama) won at Zama, and in 146 BCE Carthage was razed and its territory annexed.

Victory turned Rome from an Italian power into a Mediterranean empire — and, in the process, strained the [Republic](event:roman-republic-fall) that had won it.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Punic_Wars).

name: Battle of Cannae
summary: Hannibal's double envelopment annihilated a much larger Roman army — still studied in military academies.
body:
Part of [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars). Hannibal's double envelopment annihilated a much larger Roman army — still studied in military academies.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Cannae).

name: Battle of Zama
summary: Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal in North Africa, ending the Second Punic War.
body:
Part of [Punic Wars](event:punic-wars). Scipio Africanus defeated Hannibal in North Africa, ending the Second Punic War.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Zama).

name: Han dynasty
summary: Four centuries of Han rule set the pattern of Chinese imperial government and gave the majority ethnic group its name.
body:
The Han institutionalised [Confucian](event:confucius) learning in its bureaucracy, opened the [Silk Road](event:silk-road), and invented paper, the seismoscope and the wheelbarrow.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Han_dynasty).

name: Silk Road trade network
summary: Caravan routes linked China, Central Asia, Persia, India and the Mediterranean for some fifteen centuries.
body:
Silk, spices, paper, gunpowder, religions and — devastatingly — the [Black Death](event:black-death) all travelled these roads. The Han envoy Zhang Qian's mission west is the conventional starting point.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silk_Road).

name: Caesar's conquest of Gaul
summary: Eight years of campaigning brought Gaul under Roman rule and gave Caesar the army with which he seized power.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). Eight years of campaigning brought Gaul under Roman rule and gave Caesar the army with which he seized power.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallic_Wars).

name: Fall of the Roman Republic
summary: Civil war destroyed the republican constitution and left one man in charge of the Roman world.
body:
Caesar [crossed the Rubicon](event:rubicon) in 49 BCE, won the civil war, and was [assassinated](event:caesar-assassination) in 44. The wars that followed ended at [Actium](event:actium), leaving Octavian sole ruler and founding the [Empire](event:roman-empire).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crisis_of_the_Roman_Republic).

name: Caesar crosses the Rubicon
summary: Bringing a legion into Italy proper was an act of war against the Senate; Caesar did it anyway.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). Bringing a legion into Italy proper was an act of war against the Senate; Caesar did it anyway.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rubicon).

name: Assassination of Julius Caesar
summary: Sixty senators stabbed the dictator to death at the Theatre of Pompey on the Ides of March, 44 BCE.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). The plot to save the Republic destroyed it: the resulting civil wars ended with Octavian as sole ruler.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Assassination_of_Julius_Caesar).

name: Battle of Actium
summary: Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra off western Greece; Egypt was annexed the following year.
body:
Part of [Fall of the Roman Republic](event:roman-republic-fall). Octavian's fleet defeated Antony and Cleopatra off western Greece; Egypt was annexed the following year.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Actium).

name: Founding of the Roman Empire
summary: The Senate granted Octavian the name Augustus and effective sole power, beginning two centuries of Roman peace.
body:
The *Pax Romana* united the Mediterranean under one law, one currency and a road network that would not be matched in Europe for well over a millennium.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire).

name: Crucifixion of Jesus
summary: Jesus of Nazareth was executed in Roman Judaea; his followers' claim that he rose again founded Christianity.
body:
Within three centuries the movement had spread across the empire that killed him, and after [Constantine](event:constantine) it became the religion of the Roman state.

Christianity is today the largest religion in the world, and the Western calendar still counts from an estimate of his birth.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crucifixion_of_Jesus).

name: Eruption of Vesuvius destroys Pompeii
summary: A Plinian eruption buried Pompeii and Herculaneum under metres of ash and pyroclastic flow.
body:
Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay and left the first detailed description of a volcanic eruption. The buried towns preserve Roman daily life in unmatched detail — graffiti, bread, furniture and the voids left by the dead.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eruption_of_Mount_Vesuvius_in_79_AD).

name: Roman Empire at its greatest extent
summary: Under Trajan the empire reached from Britain to Mesopotamia, ruling perhaps a fifth of humanity.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). Under Trajan the empire reached from Britain to Mesopotamia, ruling perhaps a fifth of humanity.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trajan).

name: Antonine Plague
summary: An epidemic, probably smallpox, killed millions across the Roman world and thinned its armies.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). An epidemic, probably smallpox, killed millions across the Roman world and thinned its armies.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antonine_Plague).

name: Teotihuacan
summary: A city of over 100,000 people in the Valley of Mexico, laid out along the Avenue of the Dead.
body:
A city of over 100,000 people in the Valley of Mexico, laid out along the Avenue of the Dead.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teotihuacan).

name: Classic Maya civilisation
summary: Maya city-states in the lowlands built stepped pyramids, tracked the planets and kept the most sophisticated writing system in the Americas.
body:
Their Long Count calendar recorded dates to the day across thousands of years. In the ninth century the southern cities were abandoned, probably under a combination of drought and warfare.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maya_civilization).

name: Gupta Empire
summary: A classical age of Indian art, literature and mathematics under the Gupta kings.
body:
Aryabhata calculated pi and the length of the year; the [decimal place-value system](event:decimal-numerals) took its mature form in this period.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gupta_Empire).

name: Decimal place-value system and zero
summary: Indian mathematicians formalised positional decimal notation with zero as a number in its own right.
body:
Brahmagupta gave rules for arithmetic with zero and negative numbers in 628. Transmitted through [al-Khwarizmi](event:al-khwarizmi) to Europe, these numerals displaced Roman ones and made modern computation possible.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hindu–Arabic_numeral_system).

name: Constantine legalises Christianity
summary: The Edict of Milan ended the persecution of Christians and set the empire on the path to a Christian state.
body:
Part of [Founding of the Roman Empire](event:roman-empire). Constantine also founded [Constantinople](event:constantinople-founded) and summoned the [Council of Nicaea](event:nicaea); by 380 Christianity was the official religion of Rome.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edict_of_Milan).

name: First Council of Nicaea
summary: Bishops from across the empire agreed the Nicene Creed, defining orthodox Christian doctrine.
body:
Part of [Constantine legalises Christianity](event:constantine). Bishops from across the empire agreed the Nicene Creed, defining orthodox Christian doctrine.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Council_of_Nicaea).

name: Foundation of Constantinople
summary: Constantine refounded Byzantium as a new imperial capital that would outlast Rome itself by a thousand years.
body:
Part of [Constantine legalises Christianity](event:constantine). Constantine refounded Byzantium as a new imperial capital that would outlast Rome itself by a thousand years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constantinople).

name: Migration Period
summary: Gothic, Vandal, Frankish and Hunnic peoples moved into the Roman provinces, remaking the map of Europe.
body:
The arrival of the Huns on the steppe set the movements going; within two centuries the western provinces had become Germanic kingdoms.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_Period).

name: Visigoths sack Rome
summary: Alaric's Goths took the city for the first time in eight hundred years, shocking the Roman world.
body:
Part of [Migration Period](event:migration-period). Alaric's Goths took the city for the first time in eight hundred years, shocking the Roman world.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Rome_(410)).

name: Fall of the Western Roman Empire
summary: The last western emperor, Romulus Augustulus, was deposed at Ravenna, ending Roman rule in the west.
body:
The collapse was gradual — a century of [migrations](event:migration-period), civil wars and lost provinces, punctuated by the [sack of Rome](event:rome-sack-410) — but 476 remains the conventional date.

Western Europe fragmented into successor kingdoms, while the eastern half ruled from [Constantinople](event:constantinople-founded) continued for another thousand years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_the_Western_Roman_Empire).

name: Reign of Justinian
summary: The eastern emperor codified Roman law and briefly reconquered Italy, North Africa and southern Spain.
body:
The *Corpus Juris Civilis* is the foundation of civil law systems across Europe and Latin America today. His reconquest was undone by the [plague](event:justinian-plague) and by war exhaustion.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Justinian_I).

name: Hagia Sophia completed
summary: The great domed church of Constantinople was the largest interior space in the world for nearly a thousand years.
body:
Part of [Reign of Justinian](event:justinian). The great domed church of Constantinople was the largest interior space in the world for nearly a thousand years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagia_Sophia).

name: Plague of Justinian
summary: The first recorded pandemic of bubonic plague killed perhaps 15–50 million people around the Mediterranean.
body:
Part of [Reign of Justinian](event:justinian). Caused by the same bacterium as the later [Black Death](event:black-death), it struck Constantinople at the height of Justinian's reconquest and helped ensure it did not last.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Plague_of_Justinian).

name: The Hijra and the founding of Islam
summary: Muhammad and his followers migrated from Mecca to Medina, founding the first Muslim community; year one of the Islamic calendar.
body:
Within a decade the new faith had united the Arabian peninsula, and within a century its armies and merchants had carried it from Spain to the Indus in the [early Muslim conquests](event:islamic-conquests).

Islam is today the second largest religion in the world and shaped law, science and art across three continents.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hijrah).

name: Early Muslim conquests
summary: Arab armies took Persia, Egypt, the Levant, North Africa and Spain within roughly a century.
body:
Part of [The Hijra and the founding of Islam](event:hijra). The Sasanian empire was destroyed outright and Byzantium lost its richest provinces at [Yarmouk](event:yarmouk). The advance into Western Europe was checked at [Tours](event:tours) in 732.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_Muslim_conquests).

links.label: The Hijra and the founding of Islam

name: Battle of Yarmouk
summary: A decisive Arab victory over the Byzantine field army opened Syria and Palestine to Muslim rule.
body:
Part of [Early Muslim conquests](event:islamic-conquests). A decisive Arab victory over the Byzantine field army opened Syria and Palestine to Muslim rule.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Yarmuk).

name: Battle of Tours
summary: Charles Martel's Franks halted an Umayyad raiding army between Tours and Poitiers.
body:
Part of [Early Muslim conquests](event:islamic-conquests). Charles Martel's Franks halted an Umayyad raiding army between Tours and Poitiers.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Tours).

name: Tang dynasty
summary: A cosmopolitan Chinese golden age of poetry, Buddhism and long-distance trade, with Chang'an the largest city on Earth.
body:
Li Bai and Du Fu wrote in this period; the imperial examination system matured; and [woodblock printing](event:woodblock-printing) appeared.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tang_dynasty).

name: Woodblock printing
summary: The Diamond Sutra, printed in China in 868, is the oldest dated printed book that survives.
body:
Part of [Tang dynasty](event:tang-dynasty). The Diamond Sutra, printed in China in 868, is the oldest dated printed book that survives.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Woodblock_printing).

name: Invention of gunpowder
summary: Chinese alchemists seeking an elixir of immortality found a mixture that burned explosively.
body:
By the thirteenth century it was in bombs and rockets; carried west along the [Silk Road](event:silk-road), it produced the cannon that would eventually bring down [Constantinople](event:fall-constantinople) and the castle.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_gunpowder).

name: Islamic Golden Age
summary: Baghdad, Córdoba and Cairo became centres of mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy.
body:
Greek, Persian and Indian works were translated into Arabic at the House of Wisdom, then extended: [algebra](event:al-khwarizmi), optics, the astrolabe, hospitals and pharmacology. Much of this learning re-entered Europe through Spain and Sicily.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islamic_Golden_Age).

name: Al-Khwarizmi and algebra
summary: His treatise on balancing equations gave algebra its name, and a Latin garbling of his own gave us "algorithm".
body:
Part of [Islamic Golden Age](event:islamic-golden-age). His treatise on balancing equations gave algebra its name, and a Latin garbling of his own gave us "algorithm".

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al-Khwarizmi).

name: Charlemagne crowned emperor
summary: The pope crowned the Frankish king emperor in Rome, reviving an imperial title in the west after 324 years.
body:
Charlemagne's realm covered most of western Europe and its court sponsored a revival of learning and a legible new script. Its division among his grandsons sketched the outlines of France and Germany.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlemagne).

name: Viking Age
summary: Scandinavian raiders, traders and settlers ranged from Newfoundland to Baghdad for nearly three centuries.
body:
They sacked [Lindisfarne](event:lindisfarne), settled Iceland, Greenland and briefly [Vinland](event:vinland), founded Dublin and Kyiv, and conquered Normandy — from which their descendants took [England](event:hastings).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Viking_Age).

name: Raid on Lindisfarne
summary: The sack of the Northumbrian monastery is the conventional opening of the Viking Age in Europe.
body:
Part of [Viking Age](event:viking-age). The sack of the Northumbrian monastery is the conventional opening of the Viking Age in Europe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lindisfarne).

name: Norse reach North America
summary: Leif Erikson's people built a small settlement at L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland, five centuries before Columbus.
body:
Part of [Viking Age](event:viking-age). Tree-ring dating of the timbers puts occupation precisely at 1021 CE. The colony lasted only a few years.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norse_colonization_of_North_America).

name: East–West Schism
summary: Mutual excommunications formalised the split between the Catholic and Orthodox churches.
body:
Mutual excommunications formalised the split between the Catholic and Orthodox churches.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East–West_Schism).

name: Norman conquest of England
summary: William of Normandy defeated Harold at Hastings and took the English throne.
body:
The conquest replaced the English aristocracy wholesale, poured French vocabulary into the language, and produced the Domesday Book — the most detailed survey of any medieval kingdom.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norman_Conquest).

name: First universities
summary: Bologna, then Paris and Oxford, organised teachers and students into self-governing corporations.
body:
Bologna, then Paris and Oxford, organised teachers and students into self-governing corporations.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/University_of_Bologna).

name: The Crusades
summary: Two centuries of religious warfare between Latin Christendom and the Muslim states of the Levant.
body:
Urban II's call at Clermont launched the [First Crusade](event:first-crusade), which took Jerusalem in 1099. Later expeditions achieved less; the [Fourth](event:fourth-crusade) sacked Christian Constantinople instead, and the last mainland stronghold fell at [Acre](event:acre-1291).

The wars deepened contact — and enmity — between Europe and the Islamic world, and brought Arabic learning and goods westward.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crusades).

name: First Crusade
summary: A Latin army marched across Anatolia and took Jerusalem after a five-week siege, massacring much of its population.
body:
Part of [The Crusades](event:crusades). A Latin army marched across Anatolia and took Jerusalem after a five-week siege, massacring much of its population.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_Crusade).

name: Fourth Crusade sacks Constantinople
summary: Diverted by Venetian debts and dynastic politics, the crusaders stormed and looted the greatest Christian city in the world.
body:
Part of [The Crusades](event:crusades). Byzantium never fully recovered, which made the [fall of the city](event:fall-constantinople) in 1453 far easier.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourth_Crusade).

name: Fall of Acre
summary: The last crusader stronghold on the Levantine mainland fell to the Mamluks.
body:
Part of [The Crusades](event:crusades). The last crusader stronghold on the Levantine mainland fell to the Mamluks.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Acre_(1291)).

name: Angkor Wat built
summary: The Khmer kings raised the largest religious monument in the world, first Hindu and later Buddhist.
body:
The Khmer kings raised the largest religious monument in the world, first Hindu and later Buddhist.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angkor_Wat).

name: Magna Carta
summary: English barons forced King John to accept written limits on royal power at Runnymede.
body:
Most of its clauses concerned feudal grievances, but the principle that the ruler is subject to law — and the promise of judgement by peers — was quoted for centuries afterwards, including by the framers of the [American constitution](event:us-constitution).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magna_Carta).

name: Mongol conquests
summary: The largest contiguous land empire in history was assembled in three generations, from Korea to Hungary.
body:
[Genghis Khan](event:genghis-khan) united the steppe tribes and turned them into a disciplined army of mounted archers; his sons and grandsons destroyed the Jin, Khwarazmian and Abbasid states — [Baghdad](event:baghdad-1258) in 1258 — and founded the [Yuan dynasty](event:yuan-dynasty) in China.

The destruction was immense, but the *Pax Mongolica* also made Eurasia briefly safe for travellers like [Marco Polo](event:marco-polo) — and for the [plague](event:black-death).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mongol_conquests).

name: Genghis Khan proclaimed
summary: Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and was acclaimed universal ruler at a kurultai on the Onon river.
body:
Part of [Mongol conquests](event:mongol-conquests). Temüjin united the Mongol tribes and was acclaimed universal ruler at a kurultai on the Onon river.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genghis_Khan).

name: Mongol sack of Baghdad
summary: Hulagu's army destroyed the Abbasid capital, killed the caliph and ended the [Islamic Golden Age](event:islamic-golden-age) in Iraq.
body:
Part of [Mongol conquests](event:mongol-conquests). Hulagu's army destroyed the Abbasid capital, killed the caliph and ended the [Islamic Golden Age](event:islamic-golden-age) in Iraq.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Baghdad_(1258)).

name: Yuan dynasty founded
summary: Kublai Khan completed the conquest of Song China and ruled it as a Chinese emperor from Dadu, modern Beijing.
body:
Part of [Mongol conquests](event:mongol-conquests). Kublai Khan completed the conquest of Song China and ruled it as a Chinese emperor from Dadu, modern Beijing.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yuan_dynasty).

name: Travels of Marco Polo
summary: A Venetian merchant's account of twenty years in Asia became medieval Europe's window on China.
body:
Part of [Mongol conquests](event:mongol-conquests). The book was widely doubted, and widely read — [Columbus](event:columbus) owned an annotated copy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marco_Polo).

name: Mansa Musa's pilgrimage to Mecca
summary: The ruler of Mali crossed the Sahara with so much gold that he depressed its price in Cairo for years.
body:
Mali's wealth put Timbuktu on European maps and made it a centre of Islamic scholarship.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mansa_Musa).

name: Black Death
summary: The deadliest pandemic in recorded history killed an estimated third to half of Europe's population in six years.
body:
Plague travelled west along [Silk Road](event:silk-road) and Genoese trade routes, reaching Sicily in 1347 and Scandinavia by 1350. Contemporaries had no idea what caused it; the bacterium *Yersinia pestis* was identified only in 1894.

The survivors inherited a labour shortage that broke serfdom in much of western Europe, raised wages, and shook the authority of the Church — conditions in which the [Renaissance](event:renaissance) took root.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Death).

name: Hundred Years' War
summary: England and France fought intermittently for 116 years over the French crown.
body:
Longbows won [Crécy](event:crecy) and [Agincourt](event:agincourt), but France recovered under [Joan of Arc](event:joan-of-arc) and, with gunpowder artillery, expelled the English from all but Calais.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hundred_Years%27_War).

name: Battle of Crécy
summary: English longbowmen destroyed the French cavalry, an early sign that armoured knights were losing their dominance.
body:
Part of [Hundred Years' War](event:hundred-years-war). English longbowmen destroyed the French cavalry, an early sign that armoured knights were losing their dominance.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Crécy).

name: Battle of Agincourt
summary: Henry V's outnumbered and exhausted army routed the French in a muddy defile.
body:
Part of [Hundred Years' War](event:hundred-years-war). Henry V's outnumbered and exhausted army routed the French in a muddy defile.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Agincourt).

name: Joan of Arc
summary: A peasant girl claiming divine voices lifted the siege of Orléans and had the dauphin crowned at Reims; she was burned as a heretic two years later.
body:
Part of [Hundred Years' War](event:hundred-years-war). A peasant girl claiming divine voices lifted the siege of Orléans and had the dauphin crowned at Reims; she was burned as a heretic two years later.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joan_of_Arc).

name: Ming dynasty
summary: Native Chinese rule was restored after the Mongols; the Forbidden City was built and the [Great Wall](event:great-wall) rebuilt in the form seen today.
body:
Native Chinese rule was restored after the Mongols; the Forbidden City was built and the [Great Wall](event:great-wall) rebuilt in the form seen today.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_dynasty).

name: Voyages of Zheng He
summary: Chinese treasure fleets of hundreds of ships sailed to India, Arabia and East Africa decades before the Portuguese.
body:
Part of [Ming dynasty](event:ming-dynasty). The largest ships dwarfed anything in Europe. After 1433 the voyages were halted and the records suppressed — one of history's great counterfactuals.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ming_treasure_voyages).

name: The Renaissance
summary: A revival of classical learning and a transformation of European art, architecture and thought, beginning in Florence.
body:
Perspective, anatomy, humanist scholarship and patronage by bankers and popes produced [Leonardo](event:mona-lisa), [Michelangelo](event:sistine-chapel), Raphael and Brunelleschi's dome.

The recovery of Greek texts — accelerated by scholars fleeing the [fall of Constantinople](event:fall-constantinople) — and cheap books from the [printing press](event:printing-press) spread the movement across Europe.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Renaissance).

name: Leonardo paints the Mona Lisa
summary: Leonardo da Vinci's portrait became the most famous painting in the world.
body:
Part of [The Renaissance](event:renaissance). Leonardo da Vinci's portrait became the most famous painting in the world.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mona_Lisa).

name: Michelangelo paints the Sistine Chapel
summary: Four years of work on scaffolding produced the ceiling frescoes of the Vatican chapel.
body:
Part of [The Renaissance](event:renaissance). Four years of work on scaffolding produced the ceiling frescoes of the Vatican chapel.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sistine_Chapel_ceiling).

name: Gutenberg's printing press
summary: Movable metal type made books cheap, and made it impossible to suppress an idea once it had spread.
body:
Gutenberg combined a wine-press, oil-based ink and a mould for casting reusable type. By 1500 Europe held perhaps twenty million printed books, more than scribes had produced in the preceding thousand years.

The press carried the [Reformation](event:reformation), the [Scientific Revolution](event:copernicus) and eventually mass literacy.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Printing_press).

name: Fall of Constantinople
summary: Ottoman cannon breached the Theodosian walls and the last Roman emperor died fighting; the Byzantine Empire ended after 1,100 years.
body:
Mehmed II made the city his capital and Hagia Sophia a mosque. Greek scholars fled west with their manuscripts, feeding the [Renaissance](event:renaissance), while Ottoman control of the eastern trade routes sharpened European interest in finding a [sea route to Asia](event:age-of-discovery).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Constantinople).

name: Ottoman Empire
summary: From a frontier beylik in Anatolia the Ottomans built an empire spanning the Balkans, the Middle East and North Africa for six centuries.
body:
Its high point came under Suleiman the Magnificent; its collapse after [the First World War](event:ww1) created the modern map of the Middle East.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire).

name: The Reconquista
summary: Christian kingdoms took the Iberian peninsula from Muslim rule over nearly eight centuries.
body:
It ended with the surrender of [Granada](event:granada) in January 1492, months before [Columbus](event:columbus) sailed with Castilian backing.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reconquista).

name: Fall of Granada
summary: The last Muslim emirate in Spain surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella; Jews were expelled from Spain the same year.
body:
Part of [The Reconquista](event:reconquista). The last Muslim emirate in Spain surrendered to Ferdinand and Isabella; Jews were expelled from Spain the same year.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granada_War).

name: Inca Empire
summary: Tawantinsuyu stretched 4,000 km along the Andes, bound by roads, terraces and knotted-string records, without wheels or writing.
body:
Tawantinsuyu stretched 4,000 km along the Andes, bound by roads, terraces and knotted-string records, without wheels or writing.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inca_Empire).

name: Aztec Empire
summary: The Triple Alliance ruled central Mexico from Tenochtitlan, a lake city of perhaps 200,000 people.
body:
The Triple Alliance ruled central Mexico from Tenochtitlan, a lake city of perhaps 200,000 people.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aztec_Empire).

name: Age of Discovery
summary: European ships opened sea routes to Africa, Asia and the Americas, joining the world's hemispheres into a single system.
body:
Portuguese caravels worked their way down the African coast for decades before [Dias](event:dias) rounded the Cape and [da Gama](event:da-gama) reached India. [Columbus](event:columbus) sailed west and found a continent nobody in Europe expected; [Magellan's expedition](event:magellan) went all the way round.

What followed was the [Columbian Exchange](event:columbian-exchange), the [conquest of the Americas](event:spanish-conquest) and the [Atlantic slave trade](event:slave-trade) — the beginning of a genuinely global economy, built on immense violence.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Age_of_Discovery).

name: Dias rounds the Cape of Good Hope
summary: Bartolomeu Dias proved that the Atlantic and Indian oceans connect.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Bartolomeu Dias proved that the Atlantic and Indian oceans connect.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bartolomeu_Dias).

name: Columbus reaches the Americas
summary: Three Spanish ships made landfall in the Bahamas, beginning sustained contact between the Old World and the New.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Columbus was looking for Asia and died insisting he had found it. The consequences — [the Columbian Exchange](event:columbian-exchange), the collapse of Indigenous populations under [epidemic disease](event:americas-epidemics), and centuries of colonisation — were world-historical and, for the Americas, catastrophic.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voyages_of_Christopher_Columbus).

name: Vasco da Gama reaches India
summary: The first sea route from Europe to India broke the Venetian and Ottoman monopoly on the spice trade.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). The first sea route from Europe to India broke the Venetian and Ottoman monopoly on the spice trade.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vasco_da_Gama).

name: First circumnavigation of the globe
summary: Magellan's expedition sailed west around South America and across the Pacific; one ship of five returned under Elcano.
body:
Part of [Age of Discovery](event:age-of-discovery). Magellan himself was killed in the Philippines. The survivors proved the world was navigable in one continuous ocean — and discovered they had lost a day.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Magellan_expedition).

name: The Columbian Exchange
summary: Crops, animals and diseases moved between hemispheres, transforming diets and populations on every continent.
body:
Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cassava, chillies and tobacco went east; wheat, sugar, horses, cattle and — devastatingly — [smallpox and measles](event:americas-epidemics) went west.

The potato and maize eventually supported large population growth in Europe, Africa and China; the exchange is one reason the world could feed the [Industrial Revolution](event:industrial-revolution).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbian_exchange).

name: Epidemics devastate the Americas
summary: Smallpox, measles and typhus killed an estimated 80–95% of the Indigenous population of the Americas.
body:
Part of [The Columbian Exchange](event:columbian-exchange). Populations with no prior exposure collapsed within decades, often ahead of the Europeans themselves. The depopulation was so vast that regrowing forests may have measurably lowered global CO2 in the early 1600s.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_history_of_Indigenous_peoples_of_the_Americas).

name: Spanish conquest of the Americas
summary: Small Spanish forces, allied with rival Indigenous states and aided by epidemics, overthrew the Aztec and Inca empires.
body:
[Tenochtitlan](event:tenochtitlan) fell in 1521 and [Cusco](event:inca-conquest) in 1533. Silver from Potosí and Zacatecas then financed Habsburg Spain and flowed on to China.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_colonization_of_the_Americas).

name: Fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: After a 93-day siege, Cortés and tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan allies destroyed the Aztec capital.
body:
Part of [Spanish conquest of the Americas](event:spanish-conquest). After a 93-day siege, Cortés and tens of thousands of Tlaxcalan allies destroyed the Aztec capital.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Tenochtitlan).

name: Conquest of the Inca Empire
summary: Pizarro seized the emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, took a room full of gold as ransom, and executed him anyway.
body:
Part of [Spanish conquest of the Americas](event:spanish-conquest). Pizarro seized the emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, took a room full of gold as ransom, and executed him anyway.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_conquest_of_the_Inca_Empire).

name: Transatlantic slave trade
summary: Some 12.5 million Africans were shipped across the Atlantic in chains; nearly two million died on the voyage.
body:
The trade supplied labour for sugar, tobacco and cotton plantations in Brazil, the Caribbean and North America, and enriched ports from Lisbon to Liverpool. It depopulated regions of West and Central Africa and built the racial hierarchies of the modern Atlantic world.

Britain abolished the trade in 1807 and slavery itself in 1833; Brazil, the largest importer, abolished slavery only in 1888. See also the [American Civil War](event:us-civil-war).

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atlantic_slave_trade).

name: Protestant Reformation
summary: Western Christianity split, and with it the political order of Europe.
body:
Luther's [Ninety-five Theses](event:95-theses) were carried across Germany by the [printing press](event:printing-press) within weeks. Calvin, Zwingli and Henry VIII produced further breaks; the Catholic Church answered with the Council of Trent.

A century of religious war followed, culminating in the [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war) and the [Peace of Westphalia](event:westphalia), which established the sovereign state as the basic unit of European politics.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reformation).

name: Luther's Ninety-five Theses
summary: An Augustinian friar's objections to the sale of indulgences, addressed to his archbishop, became the spark of the Reformation.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). An Augustinian friar's objections to the sale of indulgences, addressed to his archbishop, became the spark of the Reformation.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ninety-five_Theses).

name: Council of Trent
summary: The Catholic Church defined its doctrine against Protestantism and reformed clerical discipline.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). The Catholic Church defined its doctrine against Protestantism and reformed clerical discipline.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Trent).

name: Thirty Years' War
summary: A religious quarrel in Bohemia became a general European war that killed perhaps a third of the German population.
body:
Part of [Protestant Reformation](event:reformation). A religious quarrel in Bohemia became a general European war that killed perhaps a third of the German population.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Thirty_Years%27_War).

name: Peace of Westphalia
summary: The treaties ended the war and are conventionally taken to establish the modern system of sovereign states.
body:
Part of [Thirty Years' War](event:thirty-years-war). The treaties ended the war and are conventionally taken to establish the modern system of sovereign states.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_Westphalia).

name: The Scientific Revolution
summary: Europeans replaced inherited authority with mathematics and experiment as the test of what is true about nature.
body:
It runs from [Copernicus](event:copernicus) and Vesalius through [Galileo](event:galileo), Kepler, Bacon and Descartes to [Newton's *Principia*](event:newton) — after which the same laws were known to govern falling apples and orbiting planets.

The habit of publishing, checking and repeating results is arguably the revolution's most durable product.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_Revolution).

name: Copernicus places the Sun at the centre
summary: *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium* argued that the Earth orbits the Sun, published as its author lay dying.
body:
Part of [The Scientific Revolution](event:scientific-revolution). Displacing the Earth from the centre of the cosmos was the first of the great demotions of humanity's cosmic status.

More at [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nicolaus_Copernicus).

name: Galileo turns a telescope on the sky
